name: Drafting Proposal Responses
title: Drafting Proposal Responses
answer: Drafting proposal responses covers the work of turning a request for proposal, request for information, or security questionnaire into a structured draft answer. In finance, these requests often come from institutional clients, vendors, or regulators and touch on custody, trading, risk, compliance, and reporting. The scope includes mapping each question to approved source material, assembling a first draft, and flagging gaps for a human owner. It does not include final pricing, legal commitments, or sign off, which remain with the deal team and subject matter experts.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposal responses covers the work of turning a request for proposal, request for information, or security questionnaire into a structured draft answer. In finance, these requests often come from institutional clients, vendors, or regulators and touch on custody, trading, risk, compliance, and reporting. The scope includes mapping each question to approved source material, assembling a first draft, and flagging gaps for a human owner. It does not include final pricing, legal commitments, or sign off, which remain with the deal team and subject matter experts.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The workflow runs on a document store that holds past responses, product documentation, policies, and approved language. A retrieval layer indexes those sources so an agent can pull relevant passages for each question. A large language model generates the draft, often with a template or style guide applied. The system also needs a review queue, version history, and access controls so only authorized staff can see or edit sensitive material.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The agent parses the incoming questionnaire into individual questions and classifies each by topic, such as security, compliance, or operations. It retrieves candidate answers from the approved corpus and drafts a response that cites the source passages. A human reviewer then edits, approves, or rejects each answer, and the agent records the decision for future reuse. Over time, the corpus improves as reviewers correct errors and add new approved language.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on confidentiality, accuracy, and provenance. Proposal content often includes client data, internal policies, and third party terms, so the system must respect access limits and contractual restrictions. Every drafted answer should carry a traceable source, and any claim about controls, certifications, or performance should be verified by a human before it leaves the firm. Audit logs, retention rules, and review sign offs are part of the control set, not optional extras.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter integration with deal desks and compliance systems, so drafts update as policies change. Agents will likely handle more of the first pass, including gap detection and consistency checks across a response. Human roles shift toward reviewing exceptions, owning the final language, and maintaining the source corpus. The main constraint is not model capability but trust, traceability, and the cost of keeping approved content current.
